source.title: Separable Expert Architecture: Toward Privacy-Preserving LLM Personalization via Composable Adapters and Deletable User Proxies
source.authors: Chris Schneider; P. Schoenegger; Ben Bariach

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses the difficulty of weight-based unlearning as motivation for its own personalization and deletion architecture. It evaluates proxy deletion, not recovery attacks against unlearned targeted knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization of unlearned weights, or prompt-based recovery. The deletion-verification results below are relevant to deletion generally but do not measure any listed claim version. Cited results about other unlearning methods are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a personalization architecture in which user data sits in a deletable proxy. It cites WMDP/RMU, Who's Harry Potter, NPO and SISA only to say weight-based unlearning is hard. It does not run any unlearning method, measure targeted-knowledge accuracy, or run any recovery attack (fine-tuning, direction ablation, quantization, prompting). It also does not rely on the shallow-unlearning finding as a tool, so T6/cites_only fits better than the reader's T4/uses_without_test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors say SEA sidesteps rather than solves machine unlearning, report 82–89% verification pass rates with failures attributed to generation randomness, and note a personalization–deletability tradeoff.
record.recipe_differences: No recipe for the original unlearning or recovery methods is tested; the paper proposes a separable personalization architecture with filesystem deletion of per-user proxy artifacts.
record.method_sensitivity: Verification pass rate varies with the σ multiplier: Table 3 reports results from 1.0σ through 3.0σ.

fits_no_version.finding: Omitting the per-user proxy in SEA gives outputs close to a non-personalized baseline: KL ≈ 0.21 nats, with 81.9% (Phi-3.5-mini) and 89.2% (Llama-3.1-8B) passing at 2σ. Pass rates are threshold-sensitive (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural separation of user data into a deletable adapter/steering proxy returns outputs to baseline in most cases after the proxy is removed.

record.problems: The evaluation uses four synthetic user profiles and two models at 3.8B–8B scale. The authors report degenerate near-empty outputs in some Phi-3.5-mini observations and retain them in the statistics. Verification is stochastic and threshold-sensitive; the paper itself says 11–18% of cases exceed the selected threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No results on personalization quality, cross-user contamination, or extraction and membership-inference attacks were included because they do not measure recovery of targeted knowledge after unlearning. The 2.0σ pass-rate result in Table 3 is not duplicated; it is represented in Table 2.

untested.parts: No unlearning method is evaluated on targeted-knowledge accuracy, general ability or attack recovery.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of block-versus-delete in an unlearned model.
Base models are loaded in NF4, but no unlearned weights are quantized and no recovery is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery test.
SEA claims deletion by construction but is not tested against any of the listed recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The cited unlearning works (WMDP/RMU, Who's Harry Potter) appear only in related work and motivation. The deletion here is of separately stored user-preference artifacts, not removal of knowledge from trained weights, so none of A–F applies.

versions.untested_parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy, general-ability retention, or attack recovery test of an unlearning method.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of whether an existing unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
The base models are loaded in 4-bit NF4, but the paper does not quantize unlearned weights or test whether quantization recovers targeted knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context-information recovery test.
The architecture is not tested against the listed recovery attacks; its extraction-attack privacy claims are not tests of those attacks.
